assumptions: The initial product is limited to a free owner-controlled record and a technician-reviewed battery or inverter service workflow, not a statutory product passport.
The family company can provide genuine pilot cases but does not imply external provider adoption, scalable demand, or preferential access to manufacturer data.
The stated 6-10% completion fee, 1600 PLN average transaction, 20% EBITDA margin, ownership, valuation multiple, and transaction volumes are hypotheses rather than validated economics.
Safety-sensitive diagnosis and compatibility decisions remain with qualified technicians, and manufacturer information is used only with lawful access and owner consent.

The business remains part-time only through the bounded pilot; any broader routing, verification, support, insurance, refund, and dispute workload must be delegated and funded by demonstrated contribution margin.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A time-bounded external pilot showing asset activation and fault frequency, owner-consented intake completion, provider acceptance, verified paid-job conversion, repeat provider use, average basket and take rate, and positive contribution margin after technician review, support, insurance, refunds, disputes, payments, and acquisition; plus written confirmation of lawful data access and at least one repeatable distribution partnership outside the family company.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Reframing the record as free service-context infrastructure and charging only for completed resolution is more coherent than selling a generic passport. The underlying fragmentation and orphaned-equipment problem are plausible, but the packet does not establish how often portable context changes service outcomes.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Equipment faults, warranty ambiguity, and missing service history can be urgent and expensive, while an outcome fee reduces provider risk. However, neither owner engagement nor provider willingness to surrender 6-10% of a completed job is evidenced, and actual fault frequency and lead quality are unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Payment on verified completion aligns revenue with value and avoids trying to defend a commodity passport price. Yet roughly 128 PLN revenue at the stated 1600 PLN basket and 8% fee must absorb verification, support, insurance, payments, refunds, disputes, and acquisition; none is measured. The packet's own arithmetic requires about 55,804 annual transactions for the founder-equity target, making liquidity and operating leverage binding risks.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Poland's large installed PV base supports a meaningful aftermarket search space, and choosing batteries or inverters can make the first use case narrow. Installed assets are not equivalent to addressable service transactions, however, and the best category, service frequency, basket size, and reachable provider density remain unknown.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: An owner-authorised portable history could occupy a useful cross-manufacturer position, particularly for orphaned systems. Manufacturer portals, installer suites, handover tools, DPP vendors, and the public repair platform already control adjacent workflows, and the candidate has no demonstrated exclusive data, supply, or distribution control.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A working resolution network could extend into parts, warranties, ownership transfer, provider workflow software, additional renewable equipment, and other EU markets. These adjacencies become credible only after dense case flow and lawful data accumulation, so current expansion is promising but highly contingent.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Consented configuration, service, failure, and verified completion histories could compound into a valuable proprietary dataset and workflow switching cost. Cold-start volume is unproven, owners and providers can multi-home, lawful manufacturer-data access is constrained, and incumbent platforms could add portable service intake before the dataset becomes distinctive.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Free portable records, preassembled service context, technician review, and outcome-only charging could improve convenience and trust relative to fragmented handoffs. No evidence yet shows a step-change in resolution speed, conversion, cost, or job profitability, and several existing tools already cover parts of the experience.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The 2027 battery-passport requirement, a large ageing installed base, and weaker residential new-install flow make aftermarket workflows timely. Regulation does not mandate this private service record, low-priced DPP tools limit compliance monetisation, and interoperability with statutory passports remains uncertain.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installer offers unusually low-cost access to authentic pilot cases, and wholesalers or service networks are plausible later channels. That advantage is bounded: the free record's owner activation and case generation are untested, no external channel commitment exists, and recruiting enough providers and transactions outside the family relationship may be costly and operationally dense.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's automation skills and family-company access make the closed pilot feasible within the stated time and capital. Scaling introduces technician verification, electrical and fire liability, privacy and security, provider quality, insurance, payments, disputes, and data-rights work that AI cannot remove and that conflicts with a lightly operated part-time model until delegation economics are proven.

highest_value_structural_change: Replace the prospective open marketplace with a narrow, contracted battery-service workflow for one wholesaler, manufacturer-independent service network, or insurer that supplies case flow and fulfilment capacity and pays a minimum platform/case fee. Use the family pilot only to prove the workflow, then require an external anchor contract before building broader owner acquisition or multi-provider routing.
main_structural_strength: The candidate has a credible low-cost learning wedge: real family-company cases can test a free portable record, while outcome-based charging aligns payment with a completed repair or parts transaction and accumulated service history could eventually compound.
primary_score_limiter: There is no evidence that recurring case volume and fee revenue can cover the operational cost of technician review, provider orchestration, support, insurance, and disputes at the scale required for meaningful founder wealth.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The candidate's own assumptions require about 55,804 completed annual transactions to reach the stated founder-equity objective, while transaction frequency, conversion, basket, take rate, repeat use, contribution margin, and scalable acquisition are all unvalidated and adjacent incumbents already own key records and workflows.
